words.shortDefinition: The sphere of knowledge or activity that the software is being built to serve.
words.simpleDefinition: The domain is the real-world subject area your software exists to support — insurance, logistics, e-commerce, healthcare. It includes the concepts, rules, terminology, and processes that the business operates with every day. Understanding the domain deeply is the starting point for DDD; without it, every design decision is guesswork.
words.longDefinition: Eric Evans opens Domain-Driven Design (2003) with the observation that most software failures are not technical failures — they are modeling failures. Code compiles, databases store data, services respond to requests, but the system never accurately captures what the business actually does. The domain is the problem space the software inhabits: the complete sphere of knowledge, activity, and business logic that the organisation works within. A domain is too large and complex to model all at once, which is why DDD immediately decomposes it into subdomains and bounded contexts. The domain is the unit of alignment between engineers and business stakeholders — if the team does not understand the domain, they cannot build the right model, and if the model is wrong, no amount of refactoring fixes it.
words.connector: Think of the domain like the entire rulebook of a sport — the domain is everything that makes up basketball: the rules, positions, scoring, strategies, equipment standards. Software built for basketball teams must understand all of it, not just the scoreboard.
words.techContext: Before writing a line of code the team spent two weeks in domain workshops with underwriters, learning the insurance domain well enough to draw a model both sides could reason about.
words.exampleSentence: Once the engineers understood the shipping domain deeply enough to speak the freight forwarder's language, every new feature landed correctly on the first attempt.
words.etymology: From Latin dominium (lordship, ownership) via Old French domaine; in software, Evans adopted it from its mathematical sense — the set of values or concepts over which a function or system operates.

words.shortDefinition: A simplified representation of the domain that captures only what matters for the software being built.
words.simpleDefinition: A domain model is a selective abstraction — it keeps the concepts and rules relevant to the problem at hand and deliberately omits everything else. A model for flight booking does not need to represent aerodynamics, only passengers, flights, seats, and fares. The model is expressed in code but also lives in conversations, diagrams, and documentation. In DDD, the model and the code must stay in sync.
words.longDefinition: Evans defines a model as a rigorously organised and selective abstraction of the domain. Every model is a simplification — the world is too complex to represent fully, and the goal is not completeness but usefulness. A good domain model captures the concepts, relationships, and rules that drive the software's behaviour, filtered through the specific problems the system must solve. The same real-world domain can have many valid models depending on what questions the system must answer. A model is not a diagram or a document — it is a set of ideas that finds expression in code, conversations, tests, and team vocabulary. Evans's central insight is that the model must live in the code: if the code diverges from the model, the code becomes the real model by default, and it is probably wrong.
words.connector: Think of a model like a subway map — it does not show every building, road, or alley in the city. It shows only what matters for navigating the transit system. A different transport problem (cycling routes, say) would need a completely different map of the same city.
words.techContext: The team's domain model of the loan approval process had only five key classes — Application, Applicant, CreditAssessment, Offer, and Policy — which proved far easier to evolve than the 47-table database schema it replaced.
words.exampleSentence: When the team finally aligned on a model where 'booking' and 'reservation' were distinct concepts with different lifecycles, half the existing bugs resolved themselves.
words.etymology: From Latin modulus (small measure), a diminutive of modus (measure, manner); in science and engineering, a model has meant a simplified representation of a system since the 17th century.

words.shortDefinition: A domain object defined by a unique identifier that persists over time, not by its attribute values.
words.simpleDefinition: An entity is a domain object that keeps being itself even as its details change. A Customer who moves to a new address, changes their email, and updates their payment method is still the same Customer — identified by a unique ID, not by the data they currently hold. Two entities are the same if and only if they share the same identity. This is the central distinction between entities and value objects.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the Entity concept in Domain-Driven Design (2003) to distinguish objects whose thread of identity runs through time and transformation. An entity has two defining properties: a unique identifier (UUID, database key, or business ID) that distinguishes it from all other objects of the same type regardless of attribute values, and mutable state — its attributes can change over its lifetime without affecting its identity. The classic test: if every attribute of this object changed, would it still make sense to call it the same thing? If yes, it is an entity. Entities must be modelled carefully because they carry history, invariants, and lifecycle transitions. Evans warns that assigning identity recklessly — treating things as entities when they should be value objects — adds unnecessary complexity to the model.
words.connector: Think of an entity like a person's passport — no matter how much a person changes (haircut, address, name after marriage), the passport number uniquely identifies them. The data on the passport can be updated; the identity persists.
words.techContext: We modelled Order as an entity with a UUID, which meant a customer could update shipping address and payment method without creating a new order record.
words.exampleSentence: After refactoring Customer from a plain data struct to a proper entity with a stable ID, we could finally track a customer's full history of plan changes.
words.etymology: From Latin entitas (being, existence), from ens (being), present participle of esse (to be); in philosophy, an entity is any thing that exists. Evans borrowed it to name the subset of domain objects that possess persistent, continuous existence.

words.shortDefinition: A named property of an entity or value object that describes one aspect of its current state.
words.simpleDefinition: An attribute is a named piece of data held by a domain object — a Customer's email address, an Order's total amount, a Product's SKU. Attributes describe the object's current state but do not define its identity (for entities) or its equality (for value objects, where all attributes together define equality). Choosing which attributes belong to a model — and which to leave out — is itself a modeling decision.
words.longDefinition: In domain modeling, an attribute is a named property that captures one dimension of an object's current state. Attributes are the data a domain object carries: a User has a username and a registered-at timestamp; an Invoice has a due date and a total amount. The critical DDD insight about attributes is one of omission: a good model includes only the attributes relevant to the bounded context's concerns. A Customer in the Billing context needs a billingAddress and a paymentMethod; the same Customer in the Shipping context needs a deliveryAddress and a preferredCarrier. Attributes that seem essential in one context may be irrelevant in another. Attribute selection is a distillation exercise — the model should encode the domain expert's judgment about what matters, not a reflection of every column in a database table.
words.connector: Think of attributes like the fields on a form — a rental car booking form asks for your name, license number, and return date but not your height or eye colour. The form's designer chose only the attributes relevant to the car rental domain.
words.techContext: We stripped the User entity down to six attributes for the authentication context — every other attribute lived in the separate Profile service where it belonged.
words.exampleSentence: The domain expert pointed out that delivery date and requested date were two different attributes that our original model had collapsed into one, which was the source of the scheduling bug.
words.etymology: From Latin attributum, past participle of attribuere (to assign to, attribute to), from ad- (to) + tribuere (to give, assign); in logic and grammar, an attribute is a quality assigned to a subject.

words.shortDefinition: An association between domain objects that expresses how they interact or depend on each other.
words.simpleDefinition: A relationship in a domain model is a named link between two objects that carries meaning from the domain — an Order belongs to a Customer, a Product is part of a Catalog, a Doctor treats Patients. Unlike database foreign keys, domain relationships should capture the business meaning of the association, including its directionality, multiplicity, and the obligations it creates. Evans advises modeling relationships sparingly — every unnecessary association adds complexity and coupling.
words.longDefinition: Evans devotes careful attention to relationships in Domain-Driven Design because poorly modeled associations are one of the fastest routes to an unmaintainable model. Every relationship in the domain model implies a traversal path in the code — if Order knows about Customer and Customer knows about all their Orders, both directions must be maintained consistently. The DDD practice is to challenge every bidirectional relationship: is the reverse direction actually needed in this bounded context? Most of the time, one direction suffices, and the simplification dramatically reduces coordination complexity. Relationships also have multiplicity constraints (one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-many) that the domain expert can usually specify — an Employee belongs to exactly one Department at a time, an Invoice line item references exactly one Product. These constraints belong in the model, not just the database schema.
words.connector: Think of relationships like org-chart lines — they show who reports to whom, but a good org chart only draws the lines that matter for the org's current structure. Drawing every possible interaction would produce a tangled mess, not a useful map.
words.techContext: We made the Product-to-Category relationship unidirectional: a Product knows its Category but a Category does not traverse back to all its Products, which eliminated a painful N+1 query problem.
words.exampleSentence: Once we noticed the bidirectional relationship between Patient and Appointment was only ever traversed from Patient to Appointment in practice, removing the reverse direction simplified the aggregate boundary considerably.
words.etymology: From relation (from Latin relatio, a carrying back, reference) + -ship (forming nouns of state or condition); the logical sense of a relation between concepts dates to Aristotle's Categories.

words.shortDefinition: The rules, policies, and calculations that encode how the business actually operates, independent of any technology.
words.simpleDefinition: Business logic is the part of your software that would still be true if you ripped out the database, the web framework, and the UI — it is the actual rules of how the business works. Can a customer place an order if their account is suspended? How is a discount calculated? When does an insurance claim expire? Those answers are business logic. DDD's central mission is to capture business logic in a clean domain model rather than scattering it across HTTP handlers, database queries, and service classes.
words.longDefinition: Business logic — also called domain logic — is the set of rules, constraints, workflows, and calculations that encode how the organisation operates its business. It is the most valuable and most volatile part of software: valuable because it is the competitive differentiator that makes the software useful, volatile because the business changes and the logic must change with it. The central complaint DDD addresses is that business logic is almost always found in the wrong place: buried in SQL stored procedures, scattered across controller methods, duplicated in UI validation, embedded in batch jobs. When logic lives everywhere, it becomes impossible to find, impossible to test in isolation, and catastrophically easy to get wrong by changing one copy but not another. DDD's prescription is to centralise business logic in the domain model — in entities, value objects, aggregates, and domain services — where it can be tested without infrastructure and changed in one place.
words.connector: Think of business logic like the rulebook of a board game — it exists independently of whether the game is played on a physical board, a mobile app, or a web browser. The rules are the same; only the delivery mechanism changes.
words.techContext: After we moved the discount calculation out of the Rails controller and into a DiscountPolicy domain object, it was testable, reusable, and for the first time, actually correct in all edge cases.
words.exampleSentence: The billing team's rules about prorated refunds were so complex that once we encoded them as domain logic with proper tests, we discovered three bugs that had existed undetected for two years.
words.etymology: Business from Old English bisignes (care, anxiety, occupation); logic from Greek logike (relating to reason), from logos (word, reason). The compound emerged in computing in the 1980s to distinguish application-specific rules from generic infrastructure.

words.shortDefinition: A specific interaction or transaction the system must support, described from the perspective of an actor achieving a goal.
words.simpleDefinition: A use case is a discrete, named thing the system can do for someone — Place Order, Cancel Subscription, Approve Loan, Reset Password. Each use case has a clear actor (who initiates it), a goal (what they are trying to achieve), and a result (what the system does in response). In DDD, use cases often map directly to application services or command handlers, and they orchestrate domain objects to fulfill the actor's goal without containing business logic themselves.
words.longDefinition: The use case concept originated with Ivar Jacobson's object-oriented software engineering work in the late 1980s and became a staple of UML-era design. In DDD, use cases play a specific structural role: they live at the application layer, one step above the domain model. A use case (or application service) receives an intent from outside — a command, an HTTP request, a message — and coordinates domain objects to fulfill it. The critical DDD discipline is that use cases must not contain business logic. They orchestrate; they do not decide. The logic of whether an order can be placed, whether a loan is approvable, or whether a subscription can be cancelled belongs in the domain model. Use cases are thin coordinators. This separation means that business logic can be tested without the application layer, and the application layer can be changed (e.g., switching from REST to gRPC) without touching domain logic.
words.connector: Think of a use case like a script for a restaurant server — it tells them how to take an order (greet the table, write down what they say, pass the order to the kitchen) without dictating how the chef cooks the food. The kitchen has its own logic.
words.techContext: We restructured our monolith so each endpoint mapped to exactly one use case class, which immediately revealed which endpoints were doing double duty — a PlaceOrder handler that was also sending emails and updating inventory.
words.exampleSentence: Separating the ApproveLeaveRequest use case from the domain rules about which requests are approvable let us unit-test the approval logic without simulating an HTTP request.
words.etymology: Use from Old French user (to employ), from Latin usus (use, practice); case from Latin casus (a falling, occurrence, case), from cadere (to fall). Jacobson coined the compound use case in his 1992 book Object-Oriented Software Engineering.

words.shortDefinition: A sequence of domain steps or decisions that move the business process from start to completion.
words.simpleDefinition: A workflow is the ordered series of actions, decisions, and state transitions that a business process moves through from beginning to end — for example, an order goes from Created to Payment Pending to Payment Confirmed to Fulfillment to Shipped to Delivered. Workflows expose the temporal and conditional structure of domain logic. In DDD, workflows that span multiple aggregates are often modelled using domain events and process managers rather than a single giant transaction.
words.longDefinition: Workflows in DDD represent the dynamic, temporal dimension of domain logic — not what objects are, but how they move and change over time. Every non-trivial business process is a workflow: a loan application moves through submission, credit check, underwriting, offer, acceptance, and disbursement. Each step may require coordination with different domain objects, different external systems, and different actors. One of the tensions in DDD is how to model long-running workflows without violating aggregate boundaries. Evans suggests that domain events — records of things that happened — are the connective tissue between workflow steps: when one step completes, it publishes an event that triggers the next. More recently, Scott Wlaschin's F# for Fun and Profit popularised modelling workflows as explicit, typed pipelines where each step's output type is the next step's input, making impossible states unrepresentable in code.
words.connector: Think of a workflow like an assembly line — a car starts as raw materials, moves through stamping, welding, painting, and assembly stations, and emerges as a finished vehicle. Each station has its own rules and outputs that feed the next.
words.techContext: Modelling the insurance claims workflow as an explicit series of states with typed transitions caught three edge cases at compile time that had previously only surfaced as production incidents.
words.exampleSentence: Once the team mapped the mortgage approval workflow on a whiteboard with the loan officers, they found four approval steps that the software had silently merged into one, causing regulatory compliance failures.
words.etymology: Work from Old English weorc (deed, action, task); flow from Old English flowan (to flow, stream). The compound workflow emerged in business process management literature in the 1970s and was later adopted by software engineering.

words.shortDefinition: A capability or constraint the system must satisfy, derived from domain needs and expressed in domain language.
words.simpleDefinition: A requirement is a statement of something the system must do or must not do, derived from the domain's real needs rather than from technical preferences. In DDD, requirements are most valuable when expressed in the language of the domain — not 'insert a row into the orders table' but 'allow a customer to place an order for an in-stock product.' Requirements written in domain language can be verified with domain experts and form the basis of acceptance tests.
words.longDefinition: Requirements in a DDD context are the articulated expectations of domain experts about system behaviour, expressed in domain vocabulary. Evans stresses that requirements written in technical or database terms ("the system shall update the customer record") are a symptom of the gap between engineers and domain experts. When requirements are phrased in domain language — the language the business uses — they can be reviewed and confirmed by non-technical stakeholders, which is a powerful form of early validation. DDD also distinguishes between functional requirements (what the system does: process a claim, reject an invalid order) and business rules (the constraints governing when and how: a claim can only be processed once per policy period, an order is invalid if it exceeds the customer's credit limit). Both live in the domain model, not in the database or the delivery layer.
words.connector: Think of requirements like the specifications a chef uses when opening a restaurant in a new city — the health code says what the kitchen must support (refrigeration, ventilation, handwashing stations). Requirements define what must be possible; the chef decides how to achieve it.
words.techContext: When we rewrote requirements in the insurance domain's language — 'a policyholder can submit at most one claim per coverage period' — the testing team could verify them directly with the underwriters without any developer translation.
words.exampleSentence: Translating the compliance requirements from regulatory language into domain model terms revealed that two separate rules in the legal document were already covered by a single invariant in our aggregate.
words.etymology: From require (from Latin requirere, to seek again, to need), from re- (again) + quaerere (to seek); requirement as a formal statement of what is needed was common in engineering specifications by the mid-20th century.

words.shortDefinition: A person, system, or role that initiates interactions with the domain to achieve a goal.
words.simpleDefinition: An actor is anything that takes action in the domain — a human user, an external system, a scheduled job, a device. Identifying actors is the first step in understanding use cases: you cannot define what the system does without knowing who is asking it to do something. Actors drive use cases; they are the initiators. In event storming, actors appear on orange sticky notes above the commands they issue.
words.longDefinition: The actor concept originated with Ivar Jacobson's use-case methodology and was adopted by DDD practitioners to anchor use cases in realistic scenarios. An actor is a role, not a person — the same human being might act as a Customer in one context and as an Administrator in another, and the system treats those roles differently. Actors can be human (Customer, Warehouse Operator, Compliance Officer), automated (Scheduler, External Payment Gateway, Data Feed Processor), or time-triggered (daily batch process, expiry checker). Clearly identifying actors is important because it surfaces hidden complexity: an Approver is a different actor from a Submitter even if the same employee sometimes does both — their responsibilities and permissions in the domain are distinct, and conflating them leads to access-control bugs and incorrect business logic.
words.connector: Think of actors like the cast list in a play — before writing the script you list who the characters are and what each character's role is. The same actor on stage does not mean the same role in the drama.
words.techContext: We discovered that 'Admin' was actually three distinct actors — ContentManager, BillingAdmin, and SystemOperator — which were hiding three different bounded contexts behind a single login role.
words.exampleSentence: When the team listed all actors in the procurement domain, they found that Supplier was both an external actor (submitting quotes) and a read-only audience (checking order status), which required two very different API surfaces.
words.etymology: From Latin actor (doer, performer), from agere (to do, drive, act); in use-case theory, Jacobson used actor to mean any entity that interacts with the system, deliberately choosing a theatrical metaphor to emphasise that actors play roles, not identities.

words.shortDefinition: A concrete example of a business situation that exercises specific domain behaviour, used to validate the model.
words.simpleDefinition: A scenario is a concrete story — who does what, under what conditions, and what should happen — used to test whether the domain model handles real business situations correctly. 'A premium customer places an order on a day the warehouse is closed' is a scenario. Scenarios written with domain experts during knowledge crunching sessions reveal edge cases the model must handle. In BDD, scenarios become executable specifications in the Given-When-Then format.
words.longDefinition: Scenarios are the primary tool for grounding an abstract domain model in reality. A model may look correct in diagrams but fail to handle the situations that actually occur in the domain. Evans encourages teams to collect scenarios from domain experts — stories about specific, concrete business events, including the awkward edge cases — and use them to stress-test the model. If the model cannot naturally express a scenario's sequence of events, the model is wrong. Scenarios also serve as the bridge between requirements and tests: a scenario written in domain language with a domain expert becomes a test written in code with a developer. In Behaviour-Driven Development (BDD), the Given-When-Then syntax formalises scenarios into executable specifications, making them living documentation. Scenarios are the vocabulary of the Knowledge Crunching sessions that produce a better model.
words.connector: Think of scenarios like flight simulator training programs — instead of abstract rules, trainers give pilots specific situations: 'You are at 10,000 feet, engine two fails, cross-wind from port.' Concrete scenarios reveal whether the training (or model) handles reality.
words.techContext: Writing three concrete scenarios with the accountant — refund before invoice due, refund after invoice due, refund on partial payment — revealed that our Account entity needed a separate CreditBalance concept we had been collapsing into the balance field.
words.exampleSentence: The scenario where a subscription is cancelled by the billing system due to failed payment — rather than by the user — exposed a gap in our Subscription aggregate that no one had thought to test.
words.etymology: From Italian scenario (scene, setting), from scena (scene), from Latin scaena (stage), from Greek skene (tent, stage building); adopted in planning and strategic forecasting in the 1950s to mean a described sequence of hypothetical events.

words.shortDefinition: A minimal, deployable end-to-end implementation that wires together every architectural layer before any real domain logic is built.
words.simpleDefinition: A walking skeleton is the thinnest possible slice of a system that connects all the layers — UI, application, domain, and infrastructure — and actually runs. It does almost nothing useful: it might accept a request, persist a trivial record, and return a response. But every layer exists and communicates. The skeleton walks before it has any muscle. Its value is forcing all integration and deployment concerns to be solved on day one, not discovered when the first real feature needs to be deployed.
words.longDefinition: Alistair Cockburn introduced the walking skeleton concept in Agile Software Development (2001) to describe a deceptively simple but powerful project-start discipline. The idea is that the highest-risk part of a software project is not the domain logic — it is all the integration glue: how services talk to each other, how data moves through the stack, how the system gets deployed, and how the pipeline runs. A team that builds ten features before connecting them end-to-end discovers these integration problems late, when they are expensive to fix. The walking skeleton inverts this: before any real feature is built, a minimal but complete end-to-end path exists. It compiles, deploys, and runs. The first story the team delivers is making this skeleton walk. In DDD projects, the walking skeleton anchors the bounded context's architecture from day one: the domain model compiles (even if empty), application services exist (even if they do nothing), and infrastructure adapters connect (even to an in-memory stub). Later iterations add domain logic incrementally, always to a system that already runs end to end. The skeleton is discarded when features replace it — it is a scaffold, not a prototype.
words.connector: A walking skeleton is like erecting the steel frame of a building before laying any walls — the final building looks nothing like bare steel, but every floor is connected, the structure stands, and you can test that the elevator shaft lines up before the walls go in.
words.techContext: On the first sprint the team delivered a walking skeleton: an iOS app that called a stubbed application service, which called a no-op domain model, which persisted an empty record — every layer wired, every deployment concern solved, domain logic to follow.
words.exampleSentence: By the end of day two they had a walking skeleton deployed to the staging environment — it accepted an order, assigned it a UUID, and returned it, which was almost nothing, but it meant all four layers were connected and the CI pipeline worked.
words.etymology: Skeleton from Greek skeletos (dried-up body, mummy); the compound walking skeleton as a software term was introduced by Alistair Cockburn to capture the paradox: a skeleton does not normally walk, but this one does — it is incomplete but it moves end-to-end.

words.shortDefinition: A policy or constraint from the domain that governs what the system must allow, reject, or enforce.
words.simpleDefinition: A business rule is a specific, enforceable constraint that comes from the domain — not a technical decision. 'An order cannot be placed if the customer's account is suspended' is a business rule. 'A claim cannot exceed the policy's coverage limit' is a business rule. These rules belong in the domain model, expressed as invariants on aggregates or as domain policies, not scattered across API handlers or database triggers.
words.longDefinition: Business rules are the specific, authoritative constraints that govern how domain operations proceed. They originate with the business — from legal requirements, regulatory mandates, contractual obligations, or competitive policy — and must be faithfully encoded in software. Evans distinguishes between business rules and technical constraints: a business rule says 'an employee cannot approve their own expense claim'; a technical constraint says 'the total field must be a non-negative decimal.' The former is domain logic that could exist even on paper; the latter is a data integrity concern. In DDD, business rules are typically encoded as invariants on aggregates — conditions the aggregate enforces every time its state changes. An aggregate that allows an invalid state transition (a cancelled order being shipped) has failed to enforce a business rule. Finding and naming business rules during knowledge crunching sessions is one of the most valuable activities in DDD, because these rules are often implicit — domain experts know them intuitively but have never articulated them.
words.connector: Think of business rules like the rules of a sport — a basketball referee enforces rules that were decided long before the game and that exist independently of any particular match. The rules govern what is allowed; the game is the domain.
words.techContext: When we surfaced the business rule that a policy can have at most one active claim at a time, we found it was being enforced in four different places in the codebase, each with slightly different logic.
words.exampleSentence: The accountants had a business rule that no credit note could exceed the original invoice amount — a rule so obvious to them they had never mentioned it, which is why our refund service had been issuing overcredits for months.
words.etymology: Rule from Old English reol (rule, regulation), from Latin regula (straight edge, rule), from regere (to rule, guide); the compound business rule was popularised in information systems literature in the 1980s by Ronald Ross and the Business Rules Group.

words.shortDefinition: A curated dictionary of domain terms agreed upon by engineers and domain experts to bootstrap shared vocabulary.
words.simpleDefinition: A domain glossary is a living document that defines, in plain language, the specific meaning of every important term in the domain. In DDD, building a glossary is often the first concrete step toward a ubiquitous language. Terms like 'order', 'booking', and 'reservation' mean different things to different people — a glossary forces the team to agree on one definition per term per bounded context, eliminating silent miscommunication.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduces the glossary as the practical starting point for building a ubiquitous language. Before teams can write code that reflects the domain, they need to agree on what the domain's words mean. A glossary is not a technical document — it is a collaborative one, authored jointly by domain experts and engineers. Each entry defines a term precisely, notes synonyms that should be discouraged, distinguishes between similar-sounding terms, and sometimes includes examples of when to use and when not to use the term. A living glossary evolves with the model: when the team's understanding of the domain deepens, definitions are updated. Teams that skip the glossary inevitably accumulate naming chaos: Customer and Client used interchangeably, Order meaning both a purchase intent and a fulfillment instruction depending on which developer wrote the code.
words.connector: Think of a glossary like the style guide a publisher gives to all their authors — it defines how specific terms should be used, what synonyms to avoid, and what each word means precisely, so that the final product reads with one consistent voice.
words.techContext: Creating a shared glossary with the legal team revealed that what engineers called a 'contract' covered three distinct domain concepts — Agreement, Policy, and Addendum — that had been incorrectly collapsed into a single class.
words.exampleSentence: The day the team posted the domain glossary on the wiki was the day the standup conversations got noticeably shorter, because everyone was finally using the same words with the same meanings.
words.etymology: From Medieval Latin glossarium (collection of glosses), from Latin glossa (foreign or obscure word requiring explanation), from Greek glossa (tongue, language, obscure word); a glossary was originally a list of rare or dialectal words with their explanations.

words.shortDefinition: The precise vocabulary of a domain that engineers and experts must align on to communicate without translation overhead.
words.simpleDefinition: Terminology is the set of specialised terms that a domain community uses to discuss its concepts. Insurance underwriters have precise terms for their trade — premium, deductible, rider, peril — that mean something specific and different from their everyday English meanings. Engineers who do not learn this terminology must constantly translate between business language and code, which introduces errors and delays. DDD insists that the team adopt the domain's own terminology rather than inventing technical synonyms.
words.longDefinition: Mastering domain terminology is foundational to DDD's knowledge crunching process. Every mature domain has a vocabulary that has evolved to express its concepts precisely — legal terminology, financial terminology, medical terminology are the most visible examples, but every business domain has its own specialised language. Evans argues that engineers who translate the domain's terminology into their own technical vocabulary (renaming 'premium' to 'monthlyFee' in code because it seems more obvious) create a silent barrier to collaboration. Domain experts use the domain terms; code uses different terms; they drift apart. The solution is to learn the domain's own terminology, adopt it in the model and the code, and push back when experts use different words for the same thing or the same word for different things. Surfacing and resolving terminological ambiguities is a high-value activity in discovery sessions.
words.connector: Think of terminology like learning to read sheet music — a musician and a music teacher can discuss a piece precisely using terms like allegro, forte, and ritardando, without describing every nuance in plain English. Shared terminology is the compression format for domain knowledge.
words.techContext: The shipping domain had different terminology in every department: what the warehouse called a 'despatch note' the finance team called an 'invoice companion' and the IT team had mapped to a 'shipment record' — a three-way mismatch that caused integration bugs for years.
words.exampleSentence: After spending a week learning the actuarial terminology, the developers stopped calling insurance events 'triggers' (a word that meant something specific to actuaries) and adopted the domain term 'incident', ending a month-long source of confusion.
words.etymology: From Medieval Latin terminologia, from Latin terminus (boundary, term) + Greek -logia (study, account of); the word entered English in the early 19th century to mean the body of terms belonging to a particular science or subject.

words.shortDefinition: The iterative loop of extracting domain knowledge, modeling it, and refining the model through collaboration with experts.
words.simpleDefinition: Knowledge crunching is the process of deeply learning a domain by working alongside domain experts — asking questions, building models together, writing scenarios, coding prototypes, and continuously refining your understanding. Evans considers it the heart of DDD: design happens by crunching knowledge, not by writing elegant code. The model gets better as the team's understanding deepens, and the code must follow.
words.longDefinition: Evans coined the term knowledge crunching to describe the intensive, iterative process of domain discovery that precedes and accompanies good domain modeling. Unlike requirements gathering — which implies a one-time handoff — knowledge crunching is a sustained loop: engineers and domain experts examine domain scenarios together, the engineer attempts to model what they hear, the model is shown back to the expert, misunderstandings surface, the model is refined, and the cycle repeats. Evans describes this as analogous to the process a scientist uses to understand a complex system: not a single observation but repeated, directed probing. Crunching produces the ubiquitous language — a shared vocabulary — and the domain model. It also produces insight: knowledge crunching sessions frequently reveal that what domain experts call two things are one concept in the model, or that what seems like a single concept is actually two distinct processes the domain has conflated for historical reasons.
words.connector: Think of knowledge crunching like the process a documentary filmmaker uses to understand a complex subject — they don't just read a briefing document. They spend weeks interviewing experts, filming processes, reviewing footage with their subjects, and revising their understanding until they can tell the story accurately.
words.techContext: Three weeks of knowledge crunching with the actuarial team produced a 12-concept domain glossary and a model sketch on a whiteboard that the lead underwriter confirmed was the first accurate representation of the risk calculation process any engineering team had ever produced.
words.exampleSentence: After two months of knowledge crunching with the port operators, the engineers finally understood that 'vessel schedule' and 'berth plan' were not synonyms — they were two separate concepts with different owners and update frequencies, and the model needed both.
words.etymology: Knowledge from Old English cnawan (to know); crunch as a metaphor for intensive processing or compression emerged in computational slang in the 1950s ('number crunching'). Evans applied the metaphor in DDD (2003) to describe the intellectual compression of domain complexity into a workable model.

words.shortDefinition: The irreducible complexity inherent in the problem domain itself — the complexity no abstraction can eliminate.
words.simpleDefinition: Essential complexity is the complexity that lives in the problem, not in your solution. Tax law is complex because tax law is complex — not because someone wrote bad code. Insurance underwriting rules, logistics constraints, healthcare regulations — these are genuinely hard, and software that solves them must be at least as complex as the problems themselves. DDD's goal is not to eliminate essential complexity but to capture it faithfully in the model without adding unnecessary accidental complexity on top.
words.longDefinition: The essential/accidental complexity distinction was introduced by Fred Brooks in his 1986 essay 'No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accident in Software Engineering.' Essential complexity is the complexity that is intrinsic to the problem domain — it cannot be reduced by better tools, better languages, or better processes, because it reflects the inherent structure of the problem itself. Healthcare software is complex because healthcare is complex. Financial settlement software is complex because financial settlement rules are complex. Evans builds on Brooks's distinction in DDD: the job of the domain model is to faithfully capture the essential complexity of the domain in code. Teams that attempt to simplify away essential complexity — flattening a three-tier pricing model into a single price field, or collapsing a multi-stage approval workflow into a boolean — produce software that cannot handle real business situations. The model must embrace the domain's complexity.
words.connector: Think of essential complexity like the complexity of chess — the rules are few, but the combinatorial depth of the game is irreducible. No amount of clever code makes chess simple; you can only build systems that handle the complexity gracefully.
words.techContext: When the new CTO demanded we 'simplify' the pricing engine, the domain expert patiently explained that the pricing had five dimensions because the contracts had five pricing dimensions — that was essential complexity, not engineering over-engineering.
words.exampleSentence: Recognising that the regulatory reporting rules were essential complexity — inherent to the domain, not to our implementation — freed the team to model them accurately instead of trying to cleverly avoid them.
words.etymology: Essential from Latin essentialis (relating to essence), from essentia (being, essence); complexity from Latin complexus (embrace, combination), from complecti (to embrace, encompass). Brooks's framing (1986) distinguished essence (what the thing fundamentally is) from accident (how it happens to be realised).

words.shortDefinition: Self-inflicted complexity introduced by poor abstractions or mismatched technology choices — the complexity that can be eliminated.
words.simpleDefinition: Accidental complexity is the complexity your team added unnecessarily — a baroque inheritance hierarchy that grew without discipline, an ORM that fights the domain model, a microservice split that added network overhead without removing coupling, a naming convention that no one understands. Unlike essential complexity (which reflects the problem), accidental complexity reflects poor decisions. DDD directly attacks accidental complexity by insisting the model match the domain, using the domain's own vocabulary, and not adding architectural layers that serve no domain purpose.
words.longDefinition: Fred Brooks introduced accidental complexity in 'No Silver Bullet' (1986) to describe the portion of software difficulty that is not intrinsic to the problem but is introduced by the development process, tools, and choices. Brooks believed that most of the remaining productivity gains in software would come from reducing accidental complexity — through better languages, environments, and methodologies. Evans applies this directly: a domain model that fails to match the domain introduces accidental complexity, because every feature requires fighting the model rather than extending it. Common sources of accidental complexity in DDD contexts include: anemic domain models (forcing business logic into service classes), incorrect aggregate boundaries (causing distributed transactions), generic repositories that expose persistence concerns into the domain, and naming that does not match the ubiquitous language (requiring mental translation at every read).
words.connector: Think of accidental complexity like traffic jams caused by poor road design — the journey itself is necessary, but the congestion is created by a badly designed interchange that forces all vehicles through a bottleneck. Fix the design, eliminate the congestion.
words.techContext: The 47-table join query to render the order summary page was pure accidental complexity — caused by a data model that prioritised storage efficiency over the domain's read model, which needed to be decoupled.
words.exampleSentence: The team spent two sprints just refactoring accidental complexity out of the payment service — an inheritance hierarchy that had accumulated six levels because no one had stopped to ask whether the sub-types actually existed in the domain.
words.etymology: Accidental from Latin accidentalis (happening by chance), from accidere (to happen to, befall), from ad- (to) + cadere (to fall); the philosophical sense of 'not essential, contingent' was already established in Aristotle. Brooks's essay gave it precise technical meaning in software.

words.shortDefinition: An anti-pattern where domain objects hold only data while all business logic lives in separate service classes.
words.simpleDefinition: An anemic domain model is a model full of data containers — classes with getters, setters, and no meaningful methods. All the interesting logic lives in 'service' or 'manager' classes that reach into these objects, extract their data, make decisions, and update them. Martin Fowler called this an anti-pattern in 2003 because it produces procedural code masquerading as object-oriented design, and it makes business logic impossible to find, test, or trust.
words.longDefinition: Martin Fowler coined the term 'Anemic Domain Model' in a 2003 blog post (the same year Evans published Domain-Driven Design) to describe the widely practised but problematic pattern of domain objects that are mere data structures. In an anemic model, a Customer class has fields for name, email, and status, but all the logic governing what a Customer can do — whether they can place an order, whether they are eligible for a discount, whether their account can be suspended — lives in CustomerService, OrderService, or worse, in controllers. The domain objects have no behaviour; they are passive data bags. The problems compound: business logic is duplicated across service classes, the same rule is enforced in three places with three slightly different conditions, tests must instantiate entire service graphs to test a single business rule, and domain experts who read the code (if they ever do) find nothing recognisable — no entities, no relationships, just data transfer objects and procedure calls.
words.connector: Think of an anemic domain model like a restaurant where all the ingredients are in the pantry but the recipes are pinned on the wall in 50 different locations. The kitchen has the food but not the knowledge — all the cooking decisions are scattered on notes that often contradict each other.
words.techContext: After three years of adding features, our User, Order, and Product classes had zero methods between them — all logic lived in sixteen service classes, and it took a senior developer two hours to find where 'what makes an order valid' was actually decided.
words.exampleSentence: The anemic domain model had made the codebase feel clean — small classes, clear separation — but validating a single business invariant required tracing execution across five services, three helpers, and a utility class.
words.etymology: Anemic from Greek anaimia (lack of blood), from an- (without) + haima (blood); Fowler used the medical metaphor deliberately — the domain model is alive but bloodless, going through the motions of OOP without the vitality that behaviour gives it.

words.shortDefinition: A domain model where objects encapsulate both state and behaviour, enforcing business rules within the domain layer.
words.simpleDefinition: A rich domain model is the DDD ideal: domain objects that know how to do things, not just hold data. An Order knows whether it can be shipped. A BankAccount knows whether a withdrawal exceeds its balance. A Subscription knows the rules for changing its plan. Business logic lives inside domain objects, expressed as methods that enforce invariants and capture domain rules. The objects protect their own state — you cannot put them into an invalid state because they refuse to allow it.
words.longDefinition: A rich domain model is Evans's alternative to the anemic model: domain objects that are responsible for their own behaviour, enforce their own invariants, and express the domain's logic directly. In a rich model, a Customer entity has methods like suspend(), reactivate(), and placeOrder() — methods that enforce domain rules (a suspended customer cannot place an order), update state correctly, and raise domain events when significant things happen. The model is 'rich' because the objects carry both the data and the knowledge of what that data means and how it can be changed. Rich models have several advantages: business logic has a home (inside the relevant entity or aggregate), tests are simple (exercise the domain object directly without infrastructure), and the code reads like the domain (order.ship() is meaningful to a domain expert; orderService.updateStatusToShipped(orderId) is not). Building a rich model requires sustained discipline: every business rule that surfaces must find its home in a domain object rather than being added to a service class.
words.connector: Think of a rich domain model like a self-contained machine — a combination lock knows its own state and enforces its own rules. You cannot open it by setting its internal gear positions directly; you must turn the dial through the correct sequence. The object controls its own behaviour.
words.techContext: After refactoring to a rich domain model, the average PR for a new business rule was 40 lines instead of 200, because the logic had a natural home and the tests were against the domain object directly.
words.exampleSentence: Switching to a rich domain model meant that BankAccount could raise InsufficientFundsError from within itself rather than relying on every caller to check the balance before attempting a withdrawal.
words.etymology: Rich in the sense of 'having abundance of something valuable' comes from Old English rice (powerful, wealthy); contrasted with anemic, a rich domain model is one full of behaviour and meaning rather than merely data.

words.shortDefinition: A person with deep knowledge of the business domain who collaborates with engineers to build an accurate model.
words.simpleDefinition: A domain expert is the person who knows how the business actually works — the underwriter, the logistics planner, the financial analyst, the compliance officer. They understand the rules, edge cases, exceptions, and history of their domain in a way no engineer can learn from documentation alone. DDD makes domain experts first-class collaborators in the design process, not requirements sources to be interviewed once and forgotten.
words.longDefinition: Evans devotes significant space in Domain-Driven Design to the relationship between engineers and domain experts, arguing that it is the central relationship in successful software development. A domain expert is not necessarily a senior manager or a requirements analyst — they are the people who do the domain work every day and know its intricacies deeply. An underwriter who has worked in insurance for fifteen years knows which risks defy simple categorisation. A supply chain planner knows which routes are unreliable during particular seasons. This knowledge is hard to elicit in requirements meetings and almost impossible to transfer completely into documentation. Evans's prescription is continuous, deep collaboration: engineers pair with domain experts to model scenarios, the experts confirm or correct the model, and this iteration runs throughout the project. Domain experts must be treated as intellectual partners, not as requirement vending machines.
words.connector: Think of a domain expert like a seasoned guide in a foreign country — they know the local customs, the hidden routes, the places tourists get lost, and the things that look harmless but aren't. You could read guidebooks, but nothing replaces having the guide beside you as you navigate.
words.techContext: Having the claims adjuster sit with the engineering team every Thursday for three months produced a model that the compliance team — who had never been involved in software before — immediately recognised as correct when they reviewed it.
words.exampleSentence: The domain expert's offhand comment that 'a claim can be partially approved in phases' — something she considered obvious — was the insight that resolved six months of confusion about why the approval workflow never quite fit the code.
words.etymology: Domain from Latin dominium (see Domain entry); expert from Latin expertus (proved by experience), past participle of experiri (to try, experience), from ex- (out) + periri (to try); an expert is literally one who has tested knowledge through practice.

words.shortDefinition: The business domain as it actually exists, independent of any software solution — what needs to be solved.
words.simpleDefinition: The problem space is the real world: the business domain with its people, rules, constraints, and goals as they exist before any software is written. Understanding the problem space deeply — through knowledge crunching, scenario workshops, and glossary building — is DDD's prerequisite to designing the solution space. Teams that skip straight to solutions build software that solves the wrong problem or misses critical domain nuances.
words.longDefinition: In DDD and strategic design, the problem space is the lens through which the business domain is analysed before any implementation decisions are made. The problem space contains subdomains, each of which can be classified by its strategic importance: core domains (where the business competes and innovates), supporting domains (necessary but not differentiating), and generic subdomains (commodity functionality that could be bought or outsourced). Analysing the problem space is not a one-time activity — as the business evolves, previously generic subdomains may become core, and core subdomains may be commoditised. The problem space analysis informs investment decisions: a core subdomain deserves a carefully crafted, deeply understood domain model; a generic subdomain might be served better by an off-the-shelf product. Evans stresses that engineers must understand the problem space before designing the solution space, because the solution's boundaries and structure should reflect the problem's natural boundaries.
words.connector: Think of the problem space like the patient history a doctor collects before prescribing treatment — the symptoms, lifestyle, previous conditions, medications, and family history. All of that is the problem space. The prescription is the solution space. Writing a prescription before understanding the problem space is malpractice.
words.techContext: The problem space analysis revealed that what the company thought was one domain — 'logistics' — was actually three distinct subdomains with different business rules and different stakeholder groups, each of which warranted a separate bounded context.
words.exampleSentence: Six months into building the new platform, the team finally mapped the problem space and discovered that their primary domain — cargo tracking — was a supporting domain, not a core one, meaning they could have bought a commercial solution instead.
words.etymology: Problem from Greek problema (obstacle, problem), from proballein (to throw forward), from pro- (before) + ballein (to throw); space in the abstract sense (a range of possibilities or concerns) comes from Latin spatium (room, extent, distance). Problem space as a technical term was popularised in AI research and cognitive science in the 1970s.

words.shortDefinition: The software design decisions made to model the problem space — bounded contexts, models, and architectural choices.
words.simpleDefinition: The solution space is where engineers live: the bounded contexts, domain models, architectures, and code that implement answers to the problem space. The solution space should reflect the structure of the problem space — if the problem has three distinct subdomains with different rules and vocabularies, the solution should have three separate bounded contexts. When the solution space mismatches the problem space (one database table tries to serve three subdomains), complexity and bugs follow.
words.longDefinition: The solution space is the set of software decisions made to address the problem space: how bounded contexts are drawn, which teams own which contexts, how contexts communicate, what tactical patterns are used inside each context, and what infrastructure serves them. Evans argues that the quality of the solution space depends almost entirely on the quality of the team's understanding of the problem space. A team with a shallow understanding of the problem draws context boundaries in wrong places, builds models that fight business rules, and accumulates accidental complexity. A team with deep domain knowledge builds a solution space whose structure mirrors the problem space — subdomains become bounded contexts, domain relationships become explicit integration patterns, core domain complexity is embraced rather than avoided. The solution space is not fixed at design time; as the team's understanding of the problem space deepens, the solution space must evolve.
words.connector: Think of the solution space like an architect's building plans responding to a site survey — the survey (problem space) reveals the terrain, soil quality, and access constraints; the plans (solution space) must work with all of those realities. Plans that ignore the terrain produce buildings that sink.
words.techContext: When the solution space was redesigned to mirror the problem space — three separate services for Procurement, Inventory, and Fulfilment rather than one monolith — the friction between teams dropped immediately because each team now owned their complete subdomain.
words.exampleSentence: The solution space that had grown organically over five years bore no resemblance to the problem space the domain experts described — a sure sign that the team had been building by technical instinct rather than domain understanding.
words.etymology: Solution from Latin solutionem (a loosening, dissolving), from solvere (to loosen, release, solve); paired with problem space in cognitive science and AI research to describe the set of possible operations and states available to solve a problem.

words.shortDefinition: A coherent, independently analysable slice of the domain used to identify strategic investment priorities.
words.simpleDefinition: A subdomain is a bounded piece of the overall domain that can be analysed independently — Billing, Shipping, Inventory, Customer Support. Evans classifies subdomains as core (where the business differentiates and competes), supporting (necessary but not differentiating), or generic (commodity functionality). This classification drives investment: core subdomains deserve the most careful modeling effort; generic subdomains might be bought off the shelf.
words.longDefinition: Subdomain decomposition is the first step of DDD's strategic design. The full domain of a business is too large and heterogeneous to model as a single unit — an e-commerce company's domain includes catalog management, search, checkout, payment, inventory, shipping, returns, fraud detection, and customer support, each with its own rules, vocabulary, and complexity. Evans introduces three subdomain types: Core Domains are the parts where the business competes and innovates — they should receive the team's best engineers and most careful modeling. Supporting Subdomains are necessary to support the core but are not differentiating — they can be built in-house with less investment or bought from a vendor. Generic Subdomains are commodity problems solved the same way everywhere (authentication, email delivery, PDF generation) — they should almost always be off-the-shelf. The subdomain analysis is a strategic investment decision, not just an architectural one: it answers where to invest modeling effort and where to move fast with commodity solutions.
words.connector: Think of subdomains like departments in a hospital — Oncology, Emergency Medicine, Radiology, Human Resources, and Cafeteria Services are all subdomains of the hospital's operation. The hospital competes on its clinical departments (core), needs HR to function (supporting), and buys its cafeteria management software from a vendor (generic).
words.techContext: After mapping subdomains, the CTO redirected three senior engineers from the notifications service (generic) to the risk modeling engine (core), where the competitive advantage actually lived.
words.exampleSentence: Recognising that identity management was a generic subdomain — solved well by Auth0 and Cognito — freed the team to spend their creative energy on the core subdomain, where the company's unique business rules lived.
words.etymology: Sub- from Latin sub (under, below, secondary to); domain from Latin dominium (see Domain entry). In mathematics, a subdomain is a subset of a domain that is itself a domain; Evans borrowed the term for DDD's strategic analysis.

words.shortDefinition: The growing distance between what the code expresses and what the domain model actually requires.
words.simpleDefinition: The model-code gap is the disconnect that opens up when the code evolves away from the domain model — when developers add features by hacking existing abstractions rather than extending the model correctly. Every time a developer patches code without updating the model, the gap grows. Wide gaps mean the code is increasingly hard to understand, bugs that look like technical failures are actually model failures, and domain experts who read the code (rarely, but crucially) find nothing recognisable.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduces the model-code gap as one of the central problems DDD exists to solve. In most software projects, a domain model is created early — perhaps as a UML diagram or an entity-relationship diagram — and then the code is written. As the software evolves, the code changes but the model does not. Eventually, the code has diverged so far from the model that the model is useless as a tool for understanding the code, and the code is useless as a guide for understanding the domain. The gap has several symptoms: new developers must build a mental model of the code from scratch because the official model is wrong; bugs that look like implementation errors are actually model errors (the code is correct given an incorrect model); feature requests require working around existing abstractions because the abstraction boundaries are wrong. Evans's prescription is model-driven design: the code IS the model, and changes to the domain understanding must immediately surface as changes to the code and vice versa.
words.connector: Think of the model-code gap like the difference between a city's official zoning map and how the city actually developed — when the map stops reflecting reality, planners make decisions based on fiction, and the consequences arrive in the real city.
words.techContext: After three years without updating the domain diagram, the gap between the model and the code was so wide that the architects used the codebase as the authoritative model, not the diagram — and the codebase had accumulated every misunderstanding along the way.
words.exampleSentence: The model-code gap was immediately obvious when the new engineer noticed that the domain model showed Customer and Account as separate entities but the code had merged them into a single User class three years earlier without updating any documentation.
words.etymology: Gap from Old Norse gap (chasm, opening); the compound model-code gap was coined by Evans in Domain-Driven Design (2003) to name the specific pathology of design documentation and implementation diverging over time.

words.shortDefinition: The DDD layer that answers what to build and where it lives — subdomains, bounded contexts, and context maps.
words.simpleDefinition: Strategic design is the big-picture layer of DDD: before writing a single class, it asks which parts of the domain are most important (subdomain analysis), where the model boundaries should be drawn (bounded contexts), how those boundaries relate to each other (context maps), and how teams should be organized around them. Vaughn Vernon called strategic design the most important — and most frequently skipped — part of DDD.
words.longDefinition: Evans organised Domain-Driven Design around two distinct layers of practice. Strategic design addresses the architecture of the entire system and the organisation of teams around it. It answers: Which subdomains are core (differentiated) versus supporting or generic? Where should we draw bounded context boundaries, and why? How do contexts integrate — through shared kernels, anti-corruption layers, or published language? Which teams own which contexts, and how do they collaborate? These are not implementation questions; they are organisational and architectural questions whose answers shape every implementation decision that follows. Getting strategic design wrong — drawing context boundaries in the wrong places, failing to identify the core domain, allowing context boundaries to erode — is expensive to fix and compounds over time. Evans wrote the strategic design chapters last and nearly cut them from the book; he later acknowledged they were the most important part. The DDD community absorbed this lesson slowly, and Vaughn Vernon deliberately opened Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013) with strategic design as a course correction.
words.connector: Think of strategic design like urban planning — it decides where residential zones, commercial districts, and parks go, what infrastructure connects them, and who is responsible for each area. Tactical design is architecture — it decides what goes inside each building in those zones.
words.techContext: The strategic design exercise revealed that three different teams were all building separate models of the same core domain concept — Customer — with no shared boundary, which explained why customer data was perpetually inconsistent across systems.
words.exampleSentence: Starting with strategic design rather than jumping into aggregate modeling saved the team six months of refactoring — they drew the bounded contexts correctly the first time because they understood which parts of the domain were genuinely separate.
words.etymology: Strategic from Greek strategikos (of a general, fit for command), from strategos (general), from stratos (army) + agein (to lead); in business and technology, strategic has come to mean high-level, long-horizon, concerned with overall direction rather than implementation detail.

words.shortDefinition: The DDD layer that answers how to model in code — aggregates, entities, value objects, domain events, and repositories.
words.simpleDefinition: Tactical design is the close-up layer of DDD: given a bounded context with a clear purpose, how do you model the domain concepts inside it? Tactical design provides the building blocks — entities, value objects, aggregates, domain events, repositories, domain services, and factories — and the rules for combining them. It is what most people think of first when they hear 'DDD', even though strategic design comes first.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the tactical patterns in Part II of Domain-Driven Design (2003) as 'The Building Blocks of a Model-Driven Design.' Tactical design operates inside a bounded context: it provides the vocabulary and patterns for expressing domain concepts in code. The core catalog of tactical patterns includes entities (objects with identity), value objects (immutable objects defined by attributes), aggregates (clusters of entities with a single root that enforces invariants), domain events (immutable records of significant occurrences), domain services (stateless domain logic that does not belong on an entity), repositories (collection-like abstractions for persisting and retrieving aggregates), and factories (encapsulated complex creation logic). The crucial DDD insight is that these patterns are not a methodology to follow mechanically — they are a vocabulary for capturing design decisions that emerge from knowledge crunching. The patterns serve the model; the model serves the business. Teams that apply tactical patterns without strategic grounding — drawing aggregates around database tables rather than domain invariants, for instance — produce code that looks like DDD but does not achieve DDD's goals.
words.connector: Think of tactical design like architecture within a building — strategic design decided the building goes here and serves this purpose; tactical design decides the room layout, load-bearing walls, plumbing routes, and electrical plan inside that building.
words.techContext: After the strategic design was stable, the team moved into tactical design for the core domain: they identified three aggregates, seven value objects, and twelve domain events in two whiteboard sessions with the domain expert.
words.exampleSentence: The team's tactical design work — choosing to model Price as a value object rather than a primitive — immediately eliminated an entire class of bugs where two prices with the same numeric value but different currencies were treated as equal.
words.etymology: Tactical from Greek taktikos (of arrangement), from tassein (to arrange); contrasted with strategic in military terminology where tactics are close-range manoeuvres executed within the framework set by strategy. Evans's usage mirrors this: tactics are the close-range, implementation-level decisions within the framework set by strategic design.

words.shortDefinition: A framework of algorithms partitioned from the domain model behind a simple intention-revealing interface, keeping domain objects expressive without exposing computational detail.
words.simpleDefinition: A cohesive mechanism is a cluster of closely related algorithms — things like routing calculations, scheduling heuristics, or financial computations — extracted from the domain model into its own object because the mechanism is too complex to live inside a domain entity without burying the entity's intent under computational noise. The mechanism exposes a simple, intention-revealing interface in the language of the domain. The entity calls the mechanism to perform the work; the entity's own methods remain expressive and readable.
words.longDefinition: Evans introduced the cohesive mechanism concept in Domain-Driven Design (2003) to solve a specific tension: sometimes the logic that must be embedded in a domain model is complex enough that expressing it fully inside an entity or value object makes those objects unreadable. A route-planning algorithm embedded in a Shipment entity, or a compound-interest calculation embedded in a LoanAccount aggregate, buries the entity's domain intent under algorithmic detail. The cohesive mechanism partitions this algorithm out into a separate framework object — one that is cohesive because all its parts work together toward a single computational goal — while the domain entity retains an expressive interface that calls the mechanism for results. The mechanism's interface is intentional: method names describe what the computation produces in domain terms, not how it is computed. A RoutePlanner interface with a method called fastestRouteAvoidingHazards() is intention-revealing even though its implementation may involve graph algorithms. Evans distinguishes the cohesive mechanism from a domain service: a domain service contains domain logic that spans multiple entities; a cohesive mechanism contains algorithmic logic that supports the domain but is primarily computational rather than policy-oriented. The mechanism is not part of the ubiquitous language — domain experts do not discuss it directly — but it enables domain objects to express their intent clearly without becoming computational notebooks.
words.connector: Think of a cohesive mechanism like a scientific calculator inside a domain model — the Inventory entity calls calculate(reorderPoint, demandForecast, leadTime) and gets the answer, without its own methods being swamped by forecasting mathematics. The calculator is a mechanism; the domain concept of reorder policy remains clear on the entity.
words.techContext: Extracting our compound-interest calculation into a CompoundInterestMechanism left the LoanAccount aggregate readable — its own methods expressed payment policy in plain domain terms, while the mechanism handled all the financial mathematics internally.
words.exampleSentence: The route-optimisation algorithm was a cohesive mechanism: too complex to embed in the Shipment entity without obscuring it, but too algorithmic to be a domain service — it lived in its own RoutePlanner object with an intention-revealing interface.
words.etymology: Cohesive from Latin cohaesus (stuck together) — the mechanism coheres because all its parts address one computational problem; mechanism from Greek mekhanismos (machine, contrivance) — it is the computational machinery that enables domain intent to be expressed without exposing algorithmic detail.

words.shortDefinition: Adopting DDD pattern names without the underlying collaboration and domain understanding that makes them valuable.
words.simpleDefinition: Cargo cult DDD is naming your classes Aggregate and Repository without doing the knowledge crunching, domain expert collaboration, and model refinement that justify those patterns. Teams end up with Entity classes that are just database rows with a fancier name, Aggregates that wrap single database tables, and Ubiquitous Language that is just the variable names from the old codebase with capital letters. The cargo is there; the plane never lands.
words.longDefinition: The term cargo cult comes from anthropologist accounts of Pacific Islander communities who, after World War II, built replica landing strips and control towers in hopes of attracting the cargo-laden planes that had brought goods during the war. They had the outward forms without the underlying reality. In DDD, cargo cult practice is pervasive: teams adopt DDD vocabulary and file structure — bounded contexts, aggregates, repositories — without doing the deep domain collaboration that gives these patterns meaning. Aggregates are drawn around database tables, not around domain invariants. Repositories are thin database wrappers, not domain abstractions. Bounded contexts are named after microservices, not domain concepts. The ubiquitous language is never built. Domain experts are never involved. The result is code with DDD names that carries none of DDD's benefits: the model does not match the domain, business logic is still scattered, and the code is harder to read than a simple CRUD app because it has an extra layer of abstraction that serves no real purpose.
words.connector: Think of cargo cult DDD like putting on a surgeon's scrubs and holding a scalpel without any medical training — the costume is right, but no surgery should be performed. The forms are present; the knowledge and practice are absent.
words.techContext: After six months of 'implementing DDD', the team had an Aggregate for every database table and a Repository for every Aggregate, but no domain expert had been involved, no ubiquitous language existed, and the business logic was still in the controllers.
words.exampleSentence: The code review revealed classic cargo cult DDD: a UserAggregate that exposed every field directly, a UserRepository that was a thin wrapper around the ORM, and a UserDomainService with thirty methods that were basically stored procedures in disguise.
words.etymology: Cargo cult from post-WWII anthropology, describing Pacific Melanesian religious movements that replicated material forms of Western cargo delivery in hopes of attracting goods. The metaphor entered software criticism via Richard Feynman's 1974 Caltech commencement address on cargo cult science and has since been applied to any practice that mimics surface forms without understanding.

words.shortDefinition: The natural vocabulary domain experts use when discussing their work — the raw material from which the ubiquitous language is refined.
words.simpleDefinition: Domain language is the vocabulary that exists in the domain before DDD practitioners arrive — the terms insurance professionals use, the words logistics planners rely on, the shorthand healthcare workers share. It is often inconsistent, ambiguous, and full of synonyms. DDD's job is to take this raw material and refine it into a precise, shared ubiquitous language that works in both conversation and code. You cannot build the ubiquitous language without first listening to the domain language.
words.longDefinition: Domain language is the starting material for the ubiquitous language — the vocabulary that already exists in the domain community, with all its richness, ambiguity, synonyms, and jargon. Insurance professionals say 'peril', 'coverage', 'rider', 'premium', 'adjudication'. Supply chain professionals say 'lead time', 'safety stock', 'SKU', 'bill of lading', 'cross-docking'. Healthcare professionals say 'episode of care', 'prior authorisation', 'formulary', 'co-pay'. Engineers who do not learn this language must constantly translate between business vocabulary and technical vocabulary, which introduces errors at every translation boundary. Evans argues that the correct direction is for engineers to learn the domain language, not for domain experts to learn engineering terminology. The team's job is to take the domain language — imprecise, sometimes contradictory, rich with implicit meaning — and refine it, resolve its ambiguities, and encode it in the model and the code as the ubiquitous language. This refinement process itself produces insights: when domain experts disagree about a term's meaning, they are often revealing a real distinction in the domain that the model must capture.
words.connector: Think of domain language like raw ore — it contains the valuable material (domain knowledge and domain concepts) but is mixed with impurities (synonym chaos, ambiguous overloading, context-dependent meanings). Refining it into ubiquitous language is the smelting process.
words.techContext: The domain language the trading desk used had 'position', 'exposure', and 'book' all meaning subtly different things depending on speaker and context — mapping these into precise definitions in the domain model took three weeks of facilitated sessions but eliminated a whole category of calculation errors.
words.exampleSentence: After spending a week listening to how the warehouse team actually talked about their work, the engineers realised that 'location', 'bin', 'slot', and 'position' were four distinct domain concepts that the existing code had collapsed into a single Location class.
words.etymology: Domain from Latin dominium (see Domain entry); language from Old French langage (speech, words, language), from langue (tongue), from Latin lingua (tongue, language). The compound domain language emphasises that every knowledge domain has its own linguistic conventions, separate from general-purpose language.
